newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU set to adopt tobacco reform proposals.
newsitem.headline: EU set to adopt tobacco reform proposals.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to propose new ways on Wednesday in which the European Union could discourage smoking while also reforming its controversial tobacco subsidies.
But it will not take any radical measures such as ending the $1-billion subsidies altogether or imposing restrictive anti-smoking legislation, EU sources said.
Thousands of EU tobacco farmers, who fear they will lose their jobs if the subsidies are cut, demonstrated around a bonfire of tobacco leaves outside the Commission headquarters on Tuesday.

The Commission is set to outline a series of options ministers should consider as they try to cut the EU's half million annual smoking-related deaths -- for example, strengthening warnings on cigarette packets and reducing the tar and nicotine content of cigarettes.

It is also likely to back Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler's plans to spend the tobacco subsidies on higher- quality products, offer buyouts to entice farmers away from tobacco and double the one percent levy on the subsidies that helps finance the tobacco public health fund, EU sources said.
But Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn and three other commissioners are still pushing for even deeper reforms and the proposals could be put to a vote, they said.

Flynn, who argues the EU compromises its public health campaign by channelling so much money to tobacco growers, would like the Commission to agree to consider phasing out the subsidies in the long run, they said.

Fischler has so far rejected that solution, arguing that ending the subsidies would put 200,000 tobacco growers and related workers out of work without cutting consumption since consumers would simply buy imported cigarettes.
Eight EU countries, led by Italy and Greece, produce tobacco, much of it low quality.

The Commission is set to adopt without controversy the other, mostly low-key set of proposals on tobacco consumption which would supplement the Commission's so-far unsuccessful effort to get EU states to ban all tobacco advertising.
Draft proposals drawn up by Flynn and seen by Reuters say the EU should, for example, consider declaring nicotine addiction a "dependency", allowing it to be tackled by EU public health programmes.
It should also consider amending EU rules to lower the maximum tar content of cigarettes and set a maximum nicotine content level.
